title: HTML Forms
subtitle: Forms, inputs, labels, buttons, text fields, select menus and form attributes.
description: Build interactive forms that allow users to enter and submit information.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 6: HTML Forms. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “HTML Forms”. The goal is to forms, inputs, labels, buttons, text fields, select menus and form attributes.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Forms collect input, but each control should have a clear label and a meaningful name. A label’s for attribute should match the input id so clicking the label focuses the right control.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 1: HTML Forms in practice
blocks.code: <form><label for="learner-name">Name</label><input id="learner-name" name="learnerName" autocomplete="name" required><button type="submit">Continue</button></form>

blocks.text: What to notice: focus on the part of the sample that demonstrates Forms, inputs, labels, buttons, text fields, select menus and form attributes. Identify the input, the operation, and the result before making changes.

blocks.question: Clicking the “Email” label does not focus its input. What should be checked?
options: Whether the label’s for value matches the input id.
Whether the input’s border is rounded.
Whether the page has an image.
Whether the form title is bold.
blocks.explanation: The label for/id relationship associates the visible label with the intended control.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The label for/id relationship associates the visible label with the intended control.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. The label for/id relationship associates the visible label with the intended control.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Build the idea step by step

The dashboard frames the practical purpose this way: “Build interactive forms that allow users to enter and submit information.” Use the examples as small experiments, not as code to memorize. A strong result is one you can explain and then adapt to a slightly different requirement.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Sample 2: HTML Forms in practice
blocks.code: <form><label for="email">Email address</label><input id="email" name="email" type="email" required><button type="submit">Save</button></form>

blocks.text: Application tip: in a real HTML project, choose names and structures that reveal the reason the code exists. Do not copy a snippet into a project without checking its assumptions and adapting it to the surrounding code.

blocks.question: A client form restricts a score to 0–100. Is that enough to trust the submitted value?
options: Yes, the browser always protects the server.
No; validate the value again at the trusted server/data boundary.
Yes, if the field is hidden.
Only if the button is blue.
blocks.explanation: Browser validation can be bypassed; server-side code must enforce data rules.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Browser validation can be bypassed; server-side code must enforce data rules.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Browser validation can be bypassed; server-side code must enforce data rules.

blocks.text: Choose input types that match the expected data and use built-in constraints to improve usability. Browser validation helps users correct mistakes, but it is not a security boundary: server-side code must validate any submitted data again.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.question: A signup form contains a submit button and a separate button to clear fields. What is a safe practice?
options: Let every button submit automatically.
Remove accessible names.
Set explicit button types for each intended behavior.
Use a link styled as a button with no destination.
blocks.explanation: Explicit button types prevent non-submit controls from unexpectedly submitting the form.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Explicit button types prevent non-submit controls from unexpectedly submitting the form.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Explicit button types prevent non-submit controls from unexpectedly submitting the form.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Apply it and check your reasoning
Use buttons with explicit types when a form contains more than one button. Keep error messages close to the fields they describe and ensure the form can be used by keyboard.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select HTML. Paste this snippet into the matching web/React editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. blocks.title: Sample 4: HTML Forms in practice
blocks.code: <form><fieldset><legend>Preferred practice</legend><label><input type="radio" name="mode" value="read"> Read examples</label><label><input type="radio" name="mode" value="code"> Write code</label></fieldset><button type="submit">Submit</button></form>

blocks.text: Before continuing, explain in your own words how this topic helps solve the dashboard goal: Build interactive forms that allow users to enter and submit information. Try one boundary case, one normal case, and one case that should be rejected or handled differently.

blocks.question: A reward begins at exactly 100 points, but the code awards it only when score is greater than 100. Which test exposes the bug?
options: Test only a score of 200.
Test a text value such as “high”.
Do not test the condition.
blocks.explanation: Boundary tests reveal whether the equality case follows the requirement.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Boundary tests reveal whether the equality case follows the requirement.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Boundary tests reveal whether the equality case follows the requirement.

blocks.question: Two validation rules must both pass before submission. Which logical structure is appropriate?
options: Use OR if either rule must pass.
Skip validation once the page looks correct.
Combine both checks with the appropriate AND condition.
Run the same check forever.
blocks.explanation: AND is appropriate when every required condition must be true.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. AND is appropriate when every required condition must be true.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. AND is appropriate when every required condition must be true.
